summary: Link-state routing protocols are hierarchical, but lower levels used for transit must expose their internal topology, which causes scaling problems. This experimental document extends IS-IS so Level 1 areas can provide transit while injecting only a minimal amount of information into the Level 2 area.

eli5.summary: A big region can pretend to be one small town on the map. Outsiders see less detail, so the map stays small and easy to read. This experiment shows how.

questions: how to reduce is-is topology exposure between levels
what is a proxy system in is-is
how does area proxy improve scaling
subtitle: Let a region hide its internal topology to reduce Level 2 route table overhead.

tldr.problem: In hierarchical IS-IS networks, when a Level 1 area must provide transit for Level 2 traffic, its full internal topology must be exposed to Level 2, causing the Level 2 link-state database to grow excessively, especially in data center topologies.
tldr.mechanism: Area Proxy abstracts a Level 1 area to appear as a single proxy system in Level 2, with one Area Leader generating a proxy LSP that represents all the connections to outside areas while hiding internal topology details.
tldr.outcome: Level 1 areas can provide transit without flooding their complete topology to Level 2, enabling hierarchical scaling in dense topologies like leaf-spine data centers.

today: RFC 9666 is an Experimental specification published in October 2024. It provides a mechanism for IS-IS networks to improve scaling in dense topologies where Level 1 areas provide transit.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem in Hierarchical IS-IS
sections.content:
IS-IS is a hierarchical routing protocol with two levels. Level 1 areas exchange routing information within their own domains, while Level 2 provides backbone connectivity between areas. Normally, when a Level 2 router needs to reach a destination in a Level 1 area, it uses an abstraction: a summary of the addresses in the area, not the full topology.

This abstraction works well when Level 1 areas do not provide transit. However, in modern data center topologies like leaf-spine Clos fabrics, a single Level 1 area often contains both leaf and spine routers, and Level 2 connections go to the leaves. If the spines must transit Level 2 traffic, the entire Level 1 topology (all spine and leaf links) must appear in the Level 2 link-state database.

In a large Clos fabric with many leaves and spines, this can more than double the Level 2 LSDB size and eliminates the scaling benefits of the hierarchy. RFC 9666 provides Area Proxy as an experimental solution: the entire Level 1 area appears to Level 2 as a single proxy system.
sections.eli5: Normally, maps show towns in detail. But if a town has a big network inside, you can pretend the whole town is one node on the bigger map, and only show where the town connects to other places.

sections.title: Area Proxy Architecture
sections.content:
Area Proxy introduces four classes of routers. Inside Routers are routers within the Level 1 area that run both Level 1 and Level 2 IS-IS. An Area Leader is elected from the Inside Routers to represent the entire area to Level 2. Inside Edge Routers are Inside Routers that have interfaces to outside routers. Outside Edge Routers are Level 2 routers outside the area that have adjacencies to Inside Edge Routers.

The Area Leader generates a Proxy LSP that originates from a Proxy System Identifier (a special system ID representing the entire area). This Proxy LSP appears in the Level 2 database, and all Inside Edge Routers use the Proxy System ID when sending Level 2 hellos on their outside links. Outside routers therefore see a single 'proxy system' with multiple adjacencies, rather than seeing every router inside the area.

Inside Edge Routers must filter the Level 2 LSPs generated by other Inside Routers, preventing them from leaking to the outside. Only the Proxy LSP escapes the area to Level 2.
sections.eli5: One router in the region is elected as the Area Leader. It pretends the whole region is a single router and tells outsiders about the connections to it. Routers at the edge all use the same fake name when talking to outsiders.

sections.title: Area Leader Functions
sections.content:
The Area Leader has several responsibilities. First, it learns which routers are inside the area by examining the Level 1 LSDB. All Inside Routers advertise an Area Proxy TLV (Type-Length-Value) in their Level 2 LSPs to signal participation in Area Proxy.

The Area Leader generates the Proxy LSP with the Proxy System Identifier as its source. The Proxy LSP includes information about which outside routers the inside area connects to, learned from the Inside Edge Routers' Level 2 LSPs. The Area Leader also includes routing prefixes (IPv4 and IPv6), traffic engineering information, Segment Routing capabilities, and an Area SID if segment routing is enabled.

If the Area Leader fails, a redundant candidate becomes the new Area Leader and regenerates the Proxy LSP. This looks to the outside like a normal LSP update, keeping the failure invisible.
sections.eli5: The elected leader collects information about what the region contains and tells the outside world about the region's connections and capabilities.

sections.title: Inside Routers and SPF Computation
sections.content:
Inside Routers see the full Level 1 topology and continue to use their internal area metrics. However, when performing Level 2 SPF computations, Inside Routers must follow special rules to prevent routing loops. They treat intra-area metrics (links entirely within the Level 1 area) as lower cost than inter-area metrics (links to outside). This ensures that if two paths exist with different inter-area costs, the lower inter-area cost path is always preferred, regardless of internal topology.

Outside Routers are not subject to these restrictions. When they compute Level 2 shortest paths, they use the Proxy LSP and ignore internal area structure. The cost of traversing the proxy area is zero, since only the area boundary links are visible.

The Area Proxy TLV that Inside Routers advertise in their Level 2 LSPs contains sub-TLVs: the Proxy System Identifier (distributed so all Inside Edge Routers know it) and optionally an Area SID for segment routing support.
sections.eli5: Inside routers know all the internal paths. Outside routers just see the region as one box with entry and exit points.

sections.title: Segment Routing Support
sections.content:
If the Level 1 area supports Segment Routing (SR), all Inside Routers must advertise a Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB) with the same starting value. If they disagree, the Area Leader logs an error and does not advertise an SRGB in the Proxy LSP.

The Area Leader copies Prefix SIDs and Adjacency SIDs for Outside Edge Routers from the Level 1 LSDB to the Proxy LSP. Additionally, the Area Leader can advertise an Area SID: a segment identifier that represents the entire area as an anycast address accepted by all Inside Edge Routers. This enables traffic from outside the area to use a single SID to reach any entry point into the area, improving path construction flexibility.

The Area SID sub-TLV is distributed to all Inside Edge Routers via the Area Proxy TLV, allowing them to establish forwarding based on it.
sections.eli5: The region can get its own segment identifier so that outside paths can refer to 'go to this region' and the region picks which entry point to use.

sections.title: LSP Filtering and Information Control
sections.content:
For Area Proxy abstraction to be effective, Level 2 LSPs generated by Inside Routers must not escape the area. Inside Edge Routers perform strict filtering on outbound traffic to Outside Routers:

Level 2 LSPs originating from routers found in the Level 1 LSDB are not flooded to Outside Routers. LSPs that contain the Area Proxy TLV are also filtered. Complete Sequence Number PDUs (CSNPs) and Partial Sequence Number PDUs (PSNPs) are filtered so they contain no information about Inside Router LSPs. The CSNP and PSNP source address is rewritten to the Proxy System ID if they are sent at all.

This filtering ensures that the outside area never sees the internal topology. They only see the Proxy LSP, which provides the necessary connectivity information while hiding implementation details. The filtering is transparent: both Inside and Outside routers achieve correct routing without seeing each other's full topology.
sections.eli5: At the boundary, routers throw away the detailed messages about inside routing and only pass summaries to the outside.
